title: Four times five

lines.text: Rain comes in sideways off the plateau. The monthly reassessment starts eleven minutes late because the lift is out again and Henry Gantt will not take four floors at speed.
lines.plain: Rain is blowing across the plateau. The monthly risk review starts 11 minutes late. The lift is broken again, and Henry Gantt refuses to hurry up four floors of stairs.

lines.text: Nine open, three moved since August, and I would like to be out of here by ten. R-03, the backstop is not ratified, three by four. R-05, forty administrators unavailable for retraining, three by three. R-09, the parallel run sits across an EFSF rollover, four by three, and it has said Assessing since June.
lines.plain: There are 9 open risks in the Risk Log. Three have changed since August. I would like to be out of here by 10:00. Risk R-03: the common backstop is not yet ratified, likelihood 3, impact 4. Risk R-05: 40 loan administrators may not be free for retraining, likelihood 3, impact 3. Risk R-09: the parallel run happens at the same time as an EFSF bond rollover, likelihood 4, impact 3, and its status has said Assessing since June.
g: Risk Log
the list of everything that might go wrong, with a score, an owner and a planned response

lines.text: R-07. Take it to five.
lines.plain: Now take risk R-07. Raise its likelihood score to 5.
g: likelihood
how probable it is that the risk happens, scored from 1, very low, to 5, very high
ref: Likelihood (L) A numerical value denoting the estimate of the probability that the risk will occur.

lines.text: On what?
lines.plain: Based on what evidence?

lines.text: On five. Four means the room can still decide to do nothing about it and feel reasonable.
lines.plain: Raise it to 5 because it should be 5. A score of 4 lets this meeting decide to do nothing and still feel sensible.

lines.text: That is not what the column is for. Four by five. Twenty, and it has been twenty since the thirty-first of March.
lines.plain: The likelihood column records probability. It is not a tool for pushing people to act. R-07 has likelihood 4 and impact 5. Multiply them: the risk level is 20. It has been 20 since 31 March.
g: risk level
likelihood multiplied by impact, giving a number from 1 to 25 that sets priority
ref: The risk level is the product of the likelihood and impact (RL=L*I).

lines.text: Twenty is red. Red goes to the Committee in the monthly pack and to the Corporate Investment Board on top of that. Sixteen is where that starts and we are four above it.
lines.plain: A risk level of 20 is red. Red risks go to the Project Steering Committee in the monthly report, and also to the Corporate Investment Board. The threshold for that is 16, and this risk is 4 points above it.
ref: Report: Regularly inform the Project Steering Committee (PSC) about risk-related activities.

lines.text: Writing twenty in a spreadsheet does not change what a man decides about his own career.
lines.plain: Writing the number 20 in a spreadsheet does not change what a person decides about his own career.

lines.text: No. It changes what we are obliged to do about it, and the obligation is the only part I control.
lines.plain: That is true. But the number does change what the project must do about the risk. That obligation is the only part the Project Manager controls.
ref: Medium to high level risks are dealt with at a higher priority level.

lines.text: While we are in the log. Release 1 scored Risk at sixty-eight per cent, amber, on one finding. The Committee approved the response to R-07 in October last year. It is in the minutes. It is not in the Risk Log. Half a person-day, yours, and the finding is six months old.
lines.plain: While we are in the log. My Release 1 review scored the Risk area at 68 per cent, amber, because of one finding. In October 2026 the Steering Committee approved the response to R-07. That approval is in the meeting minutes but not in the Risk Log. Correcting it takes half a person-day of your time, and the finding is now six months old.

lines.text: It goes in today.
lines.plain: The Project Manager will write it into the Risk Log today.

lines.text: You said that in April. Minutes are the record of a meeting. The log is the record of the risk, and only one of those is read by somebody who was not there.
lines.plain: You said that in April. Minutes record what a meeting did. The Risk Log records the risk itself. Only the log is read by people who were not in the meeting.
ref: Control risk-response activities: The purpose of this step is to monitor and control the implementation of risk-response activities and to revise/update the Risk Log based on a regular reassessment.

lines.text: Then the fourth step, and it is the one that quietly kills projects. Strategy on R-07 is Reduce. Two actions. The key-person clause in the contract of the eighteenth of September, and fifteen person-days of knowledge transfer, task four point seven, target the eighteenth of December last year.
lines.plain: Next comes step four of risk management: checking that the planned response is actually being carried out. This is the step projects most often skip. The response strategy for R-07 is Reduce. It has two actions. First, the key-person clause in the contract signed on 18 September 2026. Second, 15 person-days of knowledge transfer, which is task 4.7 in the Work Plan, with a target date of 18 December 2026.
g: key-person clause
a contract term forcing the supplier to replace a named expert and hand over the work
knowledge transfer
planned time in which one expert teaches others what only he knows
ref: Develop a risk-response strategy: The purpose of this step is to choose the best possible strategy to meet an identified risk and to plan actions necessary to implement this strategy.

lines.text: Two of the three modules were transferred.
lines.plain: Two of the three parts of that knowledge transfer were done.

lines.text: And the third?
lines.plain: What happened to the third part?

lines.text: December was busy. January was worse. It is scheduled.
lines.plain: December was a busy month and January was worse. The third part is in the schedule.

lines.text: It is scheduled for the week of the fourteenth of February. The third one is the product configuration engine. Two people in Europe can change a pricing rule in it without breaking a repayment schedule, and Ada is not one of them.
lines.plain: It is scheduled for the week of 14 February, which has already passed. The third part is the product configuration engine, where a new loan product is set up by settings instead of new code. Only two people in Europe can change a pricing rule there without damaging a repayment schedule. Ada Lovelace is not one of them.

lines.text: So we have a response and we have not exercised it. Nine months past its target date, on the risk at the top of the log.
lines.plain: So the project has a planned response but has not carried it out. It is nine months past its target date, and it belongs to the highest risk in the log.

lines.text: Write it at five and somebody upstairs makes him give me the fortnight.
lines.plain: If you record the likelihood as 5, senior management will force Leonardo to give me the two weeks I need.

lines.text: I am not scoring a risk to win an argument about a calendar.
lines.plain: I will not change a risk score in order to win an argument about the schedule.

lines.text: Last one and I will save it. R-11, the Levallois accelerators, six weeks down to four on a new instrument. It is still sitting at Proposed and somebody has typed Reduce in the strategy column.
lines.plain: One more before saving. Risk R-11 is about tools from Levallois Systems that could reduce onboarding of a new lending product from 6 weeks to 4. Its status is still Proposed, and somebody has entered Reduce as its response strategy.

lines.text: Enhance. It is the only good news in there and it is filed as a threat.
lines.plain: The correct strategy is Enhance. R-11 is an opportunity, not a threat, and it is the only positive entry in the log.
ref: Strategies for positive risks (opportunities): -Exploit, Enhance, Accept, Share

lines.text: Close it. Enhance is a verb that needs a person attached to it. Show me the person and I withdraw the objection.
lines.plain: Close R-11. Enhance means somebody has to do the work. Show me the person who will do it, and I will withdraw my objection.

lines.text: And R-07 stays mine.
lines.plain: And I remain the owner of risk R-07.

lines.text: The owner is whoever can act on it. On this one that was never going to be me.
lines.plain: The risk owner is the person who can actually do something about the risk. For R-07 that was never the Project Manager.
ref: Risk owner The person accountable for managing and monitoring the risk.

lines.text: The log is saved at 09:41. R-07: likelihood four, impact five, risk level twenty, escalation yes, strategy Reduce, owner Leonardo da Vinci, status Approved. On the twenty-eighth of September 2027 it is still, in every sense the guide means, a risk. Tesla leaves first and takes the stairs.
lines.plain: The Risk Log is saved at 09:41. R-07 now reads: likelihood 4, impact 5, risk level 20, escalation yes, strategy Reduce, owner Leonardo da Vinci, status Approved. On 28 September 2027 it is still a risk in the full sense of the word. Tesla leaves the room first and takes the stairs.

you.o: Project Manager. Responsible for Manage Risk; the Project Owner is Accountable for the process.
you.k: Knows the response to R-07 is nine months late and one module was never handed over.
you.w: Wants the third knowledge-transfer module done and Deming's March finding closed today.
you.f: Afraid the log is becoming a document about the project rather than a tool for running it.

tesla.o: Lead Solution Architect, seconded from Levallois into the Project Core Team. Identified R-07 himself.
tesla.k: Knows he will resign next week and that only he and one other can touch the configuration engine.
tesla.w: Wants the score raised so that somebody forces the handover before he goes.
tesla.f: Afraid he leaves and the engine leaves with him, and that it will be called disloyalty.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Risk owner of R-07 and accountable for the deliverables it threatens.
leonardo.k: Knows the third handover module was dropped twice and that his division dropped it.
leonardo.w: Wants the score left at four and Release 2 delivered on 17 December.
leonardo.f: Afraid a red risk in the Board pack becomes a question about his division, not about the risk.

deming.o: Project Quality Assurance. Reviews project quality; independent of the Project Manager.
deming.k: Knows the October 2026 approval of the R-07 response exists only in the minutes.
deming.w: Wants one six-month-old finding closed with evidence, not with an intention.
deming.f: Afraid a promise repeated every quarter is teaching the team that findings expire.

gantt.o: Project Support Office. Keeps the logs, the versions and the reassessment cycle.
gantt.k: Knows R-09 has been Assessing since June and that twenty crosses the escalation threshold.
gantt.w: Wants clean field values and the log saved before ten.
gantt.f: Afraid entries that nobody scores or closes turn the log into a filing cabinet.

note: Guide check: section 9.7, p.78. Manage Risk is a continuous cycle of four steps — identify risks, carry out a risk assessment, develop a risk-response strategy, and control the risk-response activities — plus two more that projects forget: record the response tasks in the Project Work Plan, and report regularly to the Project Steering Committee. Medium to high level risks are dealt with at a higher priority level. Risk Level is the product of likelihood and impact, RL = L x I, on a scale of 1 to 25 (p.97). Threat strategies are Avoid, Reduce, Accept and Transfer/Share; opportunity strategies are Exploit, Enhance, Accept and Share, so an opportunity filed under Reduce is a field error. The risk owner is the person accountable for managing and monitoring that risk and is frequently not the PM. RASCI: AGB I, PSC C, PO A, BM S/C, BIG C, SP I, PM R, PCT C. Approver: none — the PM maintains the Risk Log; the PSC monitors projects with high risk exposure. Pages 78 and 97.
notePlain: Rule: managing risk repeats four steps. Find risks. Score each one for likelihood and impact. Choose a response. Then check that the response is actually being carried out. Two more steps follow: put the response tasks in the Work Plan, and report risks to the Steering Committee. Medium and high risks get higher priority. The risk level is likelihood multiplied by impact, from 1 to 25. For threats the strategies are Avoid, Reduce, Accept and Transfer or Share. For opportunities they are Exploit, Enhance, Accept and Share. The risk owner is the person who must manage that risk, and it is usually not the Project Manager. RASCI: Project Manager Responsible, Project Owner Accountable, Steering Committee consulted. Nobody approves the Risk Log; the Project Manager keeps it. Pages 78 and 97.

title: The one that came true

lines.text: Gustave Eiffel is in the project room before the ceiling lights have finished coming on. He does not sit down and he does not open his laptop. There is one printed page on the table in front of him.
lines.plain: Gustave Eiffel is in the project room before the ceiling lights have fully switched on. He does not sit down and he does not open his laptop. One printed page lies on the table in front of him.

lines.text: Yesterday, sixteen forty. To me, copied to our people in Stockholm. His notice runs to the thirtieth of November.
lines.plain: He sent his resignation yesterday at 16:40. He sent it to me and copied it to our head office in Stockholm. His notice period ends on 30 November.
g: notice period
the time an employee must keep working after resigning, fixed in the contract

lines.text: Where.
lines.plain: Where is he going?

lines.text: A clearing house in Frankfurt. I telephoned him at seven this morning and offered money. It is not money.
lines.plain: He is going to a clearing house in Frankfurt. I telephoned him at 07:00 this morning and offered more money. Money is not the reason he is leaving.
g: clearing house
a company that sits between buyer and seller of a trade and guarantees that it settles

lines.text: Leonardo arrives with his coat still on and hears the last nine words of it from the doorway.
lines.plain: Leonardo comes in still wearing his coat. He hears the last part of the sentence from the doorway.

lines.text: Then buy him out. Pay him to sit in that chair until Christmas.
lines.plain: Then pay him to stay. Pay him to remain in that seat until Christmas.

lines.text: He is serving a notice, not for sale. And he is my employee, which is not the same as my asset.
lines.plain: He is working his notice period. He cannot be bought. He is an employee of Levallois, and an employee is not a piece of property.

lines.text: At twenty past eight Tesla comes in with two coffees and puts one down in front of the Project Manager. Eiffel turns the printed page face down, which is the only gentle thing anyone does all morning.
lines.plain: At 08:20 Tesla comes in carrying two coffees. He puts one of them in front of the Project Manager. Eiffel turns the printed resignation letter face down on the table. It is the only kind act of the morning.

lines.text: One of those is yours. I am not apologising for anything.
lines.plain: One coffee is for you. I will not apologise for resigning.

lines.text: Two people can change a pricing rule in that engine without breaking a repayment schedule. That has been true since January. I said so in January.
lines.plain: Only two people can change a pricing rule in that engine without damaging a repayment schedule. That has been true since January. I said so in January.
ref: Other stakeholders Identify and communicate risks in their areas of expertise.

lines.text: You said so a week ago as well.
lines.plain: He said the same thing a week ago, at the risk review.

lines.text: And you left it at four.
lines.plain: And the Project Manager kept the likelihood score at 4.

lines.text: What does it change on your screen? Say it in one sentence, because I have Florence at nine.
lines.plain: What changes in your records? Say it in one sentence, because I meet Florence at 09:00.

lines.text: R-07 asks me for a likelihood. Give me one.
lines.plain: The Risk Log entry R-07 needs a likelihood score. Give me one.
ref: Likelihood (L) A numerical value denoting the estimate of the probability that the risk will occur.

lines.text: One hundred per cent.
lines.plain: The likelihood is 100 per cent.

lines.text: The column stops at five, and five is very high. There is no value on it that means it happened on Monday at twenty to five.
lines.plain: The likelihood column only goes up to 5, and 5 means very high. No number on that scale means the event has already happened, which it did at 16:40 on Monday.
ref: 5=Very high, 4=High, 3=Medium, 2=Low, 1=Very low

lines.text: On my last project we put it at five and carried on. Nobody died.
lines.plain: On Eiffel's previous project they set the likelihood to 5 and continued as before. Nothing terrible happened.

lines.text: There is a clause. We paid for a clause.
lines.plain: There is a key-person clause in the contract. The project paid for it.

lines.text: There is, and it worked in April. It names the platform architect in our delivery organisation and it got you a replacement and three weeks of handover at our cost. Nikola is on framework days, seconded into your team. The clause was drafted before he was ever on this project.
lines.plain: The clause exists and it worked in April. It covers the platform architect employed in Levallois's delivery team. In April it produced a replacement and three weeks of handover, paid by Levallois. Tesla is different: he works under framework day-rates and is seconded into the ESM team. The clause was written before he joined this project.
g: secondment
lending an employee to another organisation for a period, while keeping their contract
ref: Develop a risk-response strategy: The purpose of this step is to choose the best possible strategy to meet an identified risk and to plan actions necessary to implement this strategy.

lines.text: Half of your mitigation was a man. Men resign. It is in the literature.
lines.plain: Half of your response to this risk was one person, and that person was me. People resign. That is well known.
ref: Control risk-response activities: The purpose of this step is to monitor and control the implementation of risk-response activities and to revise/update the Risk Log based on a regular reassessment.

lines.text: Urgency five. Impact five, because the seventeenth of December is behind it and the parallel run is behind that. Size four.
lines.plain: The Project Manager scores the new issue. Urgency 5. Impact 5, because Release 2 on 17 December depends on it, and the parallel run depends on Release 2. Size 4.
g: size (issue log)
how much effort resolving the issue will take, scored 1 to 5; not how bad it is
ref: Size Issue size represents the effort needed to resolve the issue.

lines.text: Forty person-days. That is not wrong. It is optimistic.
lines.plain: Size 4 means about 40 person-days of work. That estimate is not incorrect, but it is hopeful.

lines.text: Then here is what I want. Leave R-07 where it is until the fifteenth of November. If Levallois names somebody, the risk was managed, and nobody upstairs is told the same bad news twice.
lines.plain: This is what I want. Keep R-07 in the Risk Log until 15 November. If Levallois names a replacement architect by then, the risk was handled, and senior management does not hear the same bad news twice.

lines.text: And if they do not name anyone?
lines.plain: And if Levallois does not name anyone?

lines.text: Then you were right and it has cost you six weeks of log entries. I can live with that. Can you?
lines.plain: Then you were right, and the only cost is six weeks of extra work on the logs. I can accept that. Can you?

lines.text: The Steering Committee meets on the eighteenth. Whatever is on the screen that morning is what it will be told, and nothing else exists.
lines.plain: The Project Steering Committee meets on 18 October. It will only be told what is on the screen that morning. Anything not recorded does not exist for that meeting.
ref: Regularly report on issue status to project stakeholders (as per the Communications Plan).

choice.prompt: R-07 is on the screen at risk level twenty, and nothing in the Issue Log mentions Monday afternoon. What do you do?
choice.promptPlain: R-07 is still in the Risk Log with a risk level of 20. Nothing in the Issue Log mentions Tesla's resignation. What do you do?

options.t: Close R-07 as materialised, open I-14 in the Issue Log, put each entry's ID in the other's traceability column, escalation yes, into the pack for the eighteenth.
options.tPlain: Close R-07 in the Risk Log because it has happened. Open issue I-14 in the Issue Log. Write each entry's number in the other entry's traceability column. Mark it for escalation and put it in the papers for the Steering Committee on 18 October.

reply.text: Then write it so that in five years the two entries can still find each other. And put my name on both of them.
reply.plain: Then write it so that in five years somebody can still trace one entry from the other. And put my name on both entries.

options.why: A risk is closed once it has been managed, and materialising is one way of being managed (p.97). What is left is an unplanned event that has already happened and needs a management action, which is what the Issue Log is for; step 3 on p.79 escalates the largest and highest-impact issues to the Project Steering Committee. The traceability column of each log carries the ID of the other, so the history survives the people.
options.whyPlain: A risk is closed when it has been dealt with, and one way of being dealt with is that it happens (page 97). What remains is an unplanned event that already occurred and needs action, which belongs in the Issue Log. Step 3 on page 79 says the biggest and highest-impact issues go to the Steering Committee. Each log has a traceability column, so R-07 names I-14 and I-14 names R-07, and the history survives the people who wrote it.
ref: Escalate the largest/highest-impact issues to the Project Steering Committee (PSC) or follow the defined escalation procedure and thresholds.

options.t: Keep R-07 open and raise the likelihood to five until the fifteenth of November. He is on notice for eight more weeks and people change their minds.
options.tPlain: Keep R-07 open in the Risk Log and raise its likelihood to 5 until 15 November. Tesla works his notice for eight more weeks, and people sometimes change their minds.

reply.text: There is a leaving lunch. It is on the twenty-ninth of November and you are on the list.
reply.plain: A farewell lunch has already been arranged for 29 November, and you are on the list.

options.why: Likelihood is the estimated probability that the risk will occur (p.97); once it has occurred there is no probability left to estimate, and the twenty-five you would report is a number about nothing. It also leaves the wrong instrument in charge: a risk carries a preventive response strategy, while an issue carries an owner, an action, a size and a target date.
options.whyPlain: Likelihood means the estimated chance that something will happen (page 97). Once it has happened, there is no chance left to estimate, and a risk level of 25 would describe nothing real. It also keeps the wrong tool in use. A risk holds a preventive strategy. An issue holds an owner, an action, an effort size and a target date.
ref: Likelihood (L) A numerical value denoting the estimate of the probability that the risk will occur.

options.t: Skip the logs and raise a Change Request. Release 2 will move, and a moved baseline is a change.
options.tPlain: Do not use the logs. Raise a Change Request instead, because Release 2 will move and a changed baseline is a change.

reply.text: Nobody has asked for anything. You would be requesting a change to a date that has not moved, to fix a problem you have not written down.
reply.plain: Nobody has requested a change. You would be asking to change a date that has not moved yet, in order to solve a problem that is not recorded anywhere.

options.why: Project change management handles requested changes to the baseline, documented in a Change Request Form and the Change Log. A resignation is not requested by anyone; it is an unplanned event, so it is an issue first. Only if the resolution actually moves 17 December does a Change Request follow, and it will reference the issue.
options.whyPlain: Change management deals with changes that somebody asks for. They are recorded on a Change Request Form and in the Change Log. Nobody asked for this resignation. It is an unplanned event, so it is an issue first. If the response then moves the date of 17 December, a Change Request follows and refers to the issue.
ref: Identify issues and add them to the Issue Log.

options.t: Open the issue, but keep R-07 open alongside it for visibility until a replacement is named.
options.tPlain: Open the issue, but also keep R-07 open in the Risk Log so that the problem stays visible until a replacement architect is named.

reply.text: Then on Wednesday two people update two entries about one man, and by Christmas the two entries disagree.
reply.plain: Then every Wednesday two people will update two records about the same person, and by Christmas the two records will contradict each other.

options.why: The Closed status exists for exactly this transition: the risk has been managed, in this case by happening. Running both entries in parallel counts the same exposure twice in the Project Status Report and splits the response between a preventive action nobody can now perform and a resolution nobody has been assigned.
options.whyPlain: The Closed status exists for this exact moment: the risk has been dealt with, here by happening. Keeping both entries open counts the same problem twice in the status report. It also splits the response between prevention, which is now impossible, and resolution, which nobody has been given.
ref: Closed: This status is set once the risk has been managed

you.o: Project Manager. Responsible for Manage Risk and for Manage Issues and Decisions.
you.k: Knows R-07 materialised on 04 Oct and that the key-person clause does not cover Tesla.
you.w: Wants the transition recorded today so the Committee of 18 October sees the truth.
you.f: Afraid that holding the score at four last week cost the project its handover.

eiffel.o: Contractor's Project Manager. Reports on status and progress to the PM, and to the PSC if needed.
eiffel.k: Knows the clause covers his delivery organisation and not a framework secondment.
eiffel.w: Wants the news given straight before Stockholm manages it for him.
eiffel.f: Afraid the client concludes that Levallois cannot hold on to architects.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Risk owner of R-07 and, from today, owner of the issue it becomes.
leonardo.k: Knows two of three handover modules were done and which one was not.
leonardo.w: Wants six weeks of quiet before the Committee is told anything.
leonardo.f: Afraid of standing in front of the Committee twice with the same bad news.

tesla.o: Lead Solution Architect on the Project Core Team, working a notice period to 30 Nov 2027.
tesla.k: Knows exactly what leaves the building with him, module by module.
tesla.w: Wants it stated plainly that he warned them in January and again last week.
tesla.f: Afraid the configuration engine becomes a thing nobody dares to change.

note: Guide check: section 9.8, p.79, and the boundary PM² tests hardest. A risk may happen; an issue has already happened; a change deliberately alters an approved baseline. When R-07 materialises, the Risk Log entry moves to Closed — the status set once a risk has been managed (p.97) — and Issue Log entry I-14 is opened, with each traceability column naming the other. Issues are scored on urgency, impact and size as three separate values: there is no L x I product outside the Risk Log, and size measures effort to resolve, not severity (p.98). Step 3 escalates the largest and highest-impact issues to the Project Steering Committee, or follows the project's own escalation thresholds. RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM S, BIG C, SP I, PM R, PCT C. Approver: none — the PM maintains the Issue Log; the PSC is the escalation destination, which is not the same thing as being Accountable. Pages 79, 97 and 98.
notePlain: Rule: this is the boundary that examinations test most. A risk might happen. An issue has already happened. A change deliberately alters an approved plan. When R-07 happens, its Risk Log entry is set to Closed, because a risk is closed once it has been managed, and happening counts. A new Issue Log entry, I-14, is opened. Each entry records the other's number, so the history can be traced. Issues are scored with three separate numbers: urgency, impact and size. There is no multiplication, and size means the effort needed to fix it. The biggest and highest-impact issues go to the Steering Committee. RASCI: Project Manager Responsible, Project Owner Accountable, Steering Committee only Informed, even though it is where issues are escalated. Nobody approves the Issue Log. Pages 79, 97 and 98.

title: What the committee is for
where: ESM, Kirchberg — Room Spaak, fifth floor

lines.text: Item three of the Steering Committee, eleven minutes allocated. Gustave Eiffel is invited for this item only and sits at the corner of the table where contractors sit.
lines.plain: This is item three on the Steering Committee agenda, with 11 minutes allocated to it. Gustave Eiffel is invited only for this item. He sits at the corner of the table where contractors sit.
g: Project Steering Committee
the project's decision and issue-resolution body, chaired by the Project Owner

lines.text: Read it as it is written. Not as you would like it to sound.
lines.plain: Read the entry exactly as it is written in the log. Do not soften the words.

lines.text: I-14. Lead solution architect resigns, last working day the thirtieth of November. Materialisation of risk R-07, closed on the fifth. Urgency five, impact five, size four. Owner Leonardo da Vinci. Target date the fifteenth of November. Escalation yes.
lines.plain: Issue I-14. The lead solution architect has resigned and his last working day is 30 November. This is the materialisation of risk R-07, which was closed on 5 October. Urgency 5, impact 5, size 4. The issue owner is Leonardo da Vinci. The target date is 15 November. It is escalated.
ref: Issues are identified, evaluated and assigned for resolution to relevant project stakeholders as per the Issue Management process

lines.text: Does the seventeenth of December move?
lines.plain: Will Release 2 slip from 17 December?

lines.text: Not yet.
lines.plain: Not at this stage.

lines.text: That is not an answer.
lines.plain: That is not a real answer.

lines.text: It is the honest one on the eighteenth of October. Ask me on the fifteenth of November and you will get an answer.
lines.plain: It is the honest answer on 18 October. Ask the same question on 15 November and there will be a real answer.

lines.text: Everyone in this room has said the word architect. Do you need a person, or do you need what is in his head by the thirtieth of November?
lines.plain: Everybody in this room has used the word architect. Which do you need: a person in the role, or the knowledge in his head, transferred before 30 November?

lines.text: Both. Only one of them is available.
lines.plain: The project needs both. Only one of the two is possible now.

lines.text: The Architecture Office offered me a design authority for eight weeks. I said no. I will not put an ESM architect inside a design ESM is buying.
lines.plain: The Architecture Office offered me one of its architects as design authority for eight weeks. I refused. I will not have an ESM architect designing a platform that ESM is buying from a supplier.
g: design authority
the person who decides how the system is built and who may change that design

lines.text: What happens to my parallel run if December moves?
lines.plain: What happens to the parallel run if Release 2 moves from December?

note: Guide check: section 9.8, p.79. The PM monitors issues and decides how to manage them; the largest and highest-impact ones are escalated to the Project Steering Committee, or follow the project's defined escalation procedure and thresholds. Decisions may be implemented by the PM or escalated to the PSC depending on their importance, and are explicitly linked to the resolution of other log items, so D-11 names I-14, which names R-07. The Decision Log records the decision, its owner, the people present, the decision date and the separate date of application, and who it was communicated to; it has no status column (p.99). RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM S, BIG C, SP I, PM R, PCT C — the Project Owner is Accountable for the process, while the PSC is where issues go. Approver: the decision owner; escalated decisions are taken by the PSC. Pages 79 and 99.
notePlain: Rule: the Project Manager watches the issues and decides how to handle them. The biggest and highest-impact issues go up to the Steering Committee, or follow the escalation rules the project agreed. Some decisions the Project Manager takes alone; important ones go to the Steering Committee. Decisions are linked to the risks, issues and changes they resolve, so D-11 names I-14, and I-14 names R-07. The Decision Log records the decision, its owner, who was present, the date it was taken, the separate date it starts to apply, and who was told. It has no status column, so it never says whether the decision worked. RASCI: Project Manager Responsible, Project Owner Accountable, Steering Committee Informed. Pages 79 and 99.

note: Guide check: section 9.13, p.85, the chapter's second RASCI anomaly: AGB A, PSC C, PO C, BM C, BIG I, SP S, PM R, PCT I — the Appropriate Governance Body is Accountable and the Project Manager Responsible. The PM manages the contractor; the Contractor's Project Manager delivers acceptable quality and reports status and progress to the PM and, if necessary, to the PSC, which fixes the escalation ladder as CPM to PM to PSC. The PQA performs most of the quality controls on outsourced work. The PSC ensures the contractor was chosen according to the organisation's processes and that contracts define both parties' expectations; the PM applies the Outsourcing Plan's working methods, monitors costs and schedules, manages changes to the outsourced work, validates interim and final deliverables against agreed criteria, and secures formal approvals on time. Outputs are unglamorous and contractual: status and progress reports, signed contracts, signed purchase orders, signed timesheets. notePlain: Rule: on Manage Outsourcing the governance body that owns the contract is Accountable and the Project Manager is Responsible. This is the second reversal in the chapter. The Project Manager manages the contractor as an organisation, never the contractor's individual staff. The contractor's project manager reports progress to the Project Manager, and to the Steering Committee if necessary, so escalation runs contractor's project manager, then Project Manager, then Steering Committee. The quality reviewer performs most of the quality checks on outsourced work. The Steering Committee makes sure the contractor was selected properly and that contracts state what both sides expect. The Project Manager applies the Outsourcing Plan, watches cost and schedule, manages changes, and checks deliverables against agreed criteria. The outputs are contractual: reports, signed contracts, purchase orders and timesheets. Page 85.

note: Guide check: section 9.10, pp.81-82. RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM S, BIG C, SP C, PM R, PCT C — the Project Owner is Accountable and formally accepts the deliverables; the Project Manager is Responsible for running the process. The domain-expert rule on p.81 is explicit: a User Representative reviews the User Manual, the support and maintenance organisation reviews the Operations Manual, the organisation responsible for training reviews training material, and service operations reviews release notes. The PSC approves the application of the acceptance strategy and schedule; the BM provides qualified resources to support the users' acceptance; the PQA assists the PM and performs most of the quality controls; the PM ensures supporting deliverables such as documentation are supplied alongside the main ones. Deliverables may be conditionally accepted even with known defects, if these are documented and there is a plan to address them. Approver: the Project Owner, on a signed Deliverables Acceptance Note. Final project acceptance takes place in the Closing Phase, not here. Pages 81 and 82.
notePlain: Rule: the Project Owner is Accountable for accepting deliverables and signs for them. The Project Manager is Responsible for running the acceptance process. Specialist documents go to specialist reviewers. The User Representative reviews the User Manual. The support and maintenance team reviews the Operations Manual. The training organisation reviews training material. Service operations reviews release notes. The Steering Committee approves the acceptance approach and schedule. The Business Manager supplies trained people to help users accept the work. The quality reviewer helps the Project Manager and performs most of the checks. Supporting documents are delivered with the main deliverable. A deliverable can be accepted with known defects, if the defects are written down and there is a dated plan to fix them. Final acceptance of the whole project happens later, in the Closing Phase. Pages 81 and 82.

Only then can the PSC authorise the move to Closing. Final project acceptance takes place in the Closing Phase, so provisional acceptance is the correct state to arrive at this gate with.
options.whyPlain: At this gate the Project Manager checks that the goals of the Executing Phase were met, that the planned work was done, that the requirements were met and the outputs delivered, and that the Project Owner has accepted the deliverables at least provisionally, completed the transition and made the outputs available to users. Only then can the Steering Committee authorise the move to Closing. Final acceptance happens in the Closing Phase, so arriving here with provisional acceptance is correct.
ref: The Project Manager (PM) is also responsible for ensuring that the Project Owner (PO) accepts the deliverables (at least provisionally), finalises the transition and makes the outputs available to the end-users.

note: Guide check: Manage Transition is section 9.11, p.83, with RASCI AGB I, PSC A, PO C, BM C, BIG C, SP C, PM R, PCT C — the Steering Committee is Accountable, the Project Manager Responsible. Where there is no separate Transition Plan the PM must still identify the roles responsible, define what must be achieved before transition is complete, prepare data backups and rollback scenarios, ensure business implementation activities and user training happen, coordinate and communicate delivery, start maintenance and support, and hand over all documentation; the PO provisionally accepts before transition completes and ownership then transfers. The RfC gate, section 7.6 p.62, is the third and final phase gate: the PM assesses that the Executing goals were met, requirements satisfied and outputs fully delivered, accepted at least provisionally, transitioned and available to end-users, and the PSC then authorises the move to Closing. The Phase Exit Review Checklist guides that assessment; nobody approves it. Approver: the PSC authorises the phase transition. Final project acceptance, the Project Acceptance Note and administrative closure all belong to the Closing Phase (pp.63 and 81). Pages 62, 63 and 83.
notePlain: Rule: on Manage Transition the Steering Committee is Accountable and the Project Manager is Responsible. If a project has no separate Transition Plan, the Project Manager must still name who is responsible, define what must be true before transition is finished, prepare backups and a rollback plan, make sure training and business changes happen, coordinate and communicate the delivery, start maintenance and support, and hand over all documentation. The Project Owner accepts the deliverables provisionally before transition is complete, and ownership then passes to her. Ready for Closing is the third and last gate. The Project Manager checks that the phase goals were met, the requirements satisfied, the outputs delivered, accepted at least provisionally, transitioned and available to users. The Steering Committee then authorises the move to Closing. The Phase Exit Review Checklist guides the check and approves nothing. Final acceptance and administrative closure belong to the Closing Phase. Pages 62, 63 and 83.
